readAloud.text: Archaeologists have long debated why the Maya civilisation abandoned its great stone cities during the ninth century. Evidence from lake sediments indicates that the region suffered a series of severe droughts lasting several decades. Combined with soil exhaustion and constant warfare between rival kingdoms, these dry periods may have made urban life unsustainable, forcing populations to migrate towards coastal areas.

Children develop language at an astonishing pace between their first and fifth birthdays. During this period, a typical child learns thousands of words and masters the basic grammatical rules of their native tongue without any formal instruction. Researchers believe that early exposure to rich conversation, storytelling, and shared reading significantly influences the size of a child's vocabulary.

Volcanoes form where molten rock, known as magma, rises from deep within the Earth and erupts at the surface. Although eruptions are often destructive, volcanic activity also creates highly fertile soils that support dense agricultural populations. In countries such as Indonesia and Italy, farmers have cultivated the slopes of active volcanoes for centuries, accepting the risks in exchange for exceptional harvests.

Every year, millions of birds undertake extraordinary journeys between their breeding and wintering grounds. Some species travel more than ten thousand kilometres, navigating by the sun, the stars, and the Earth's magnetic field. Scientists track these migrations using lightweight satellite tags, and their data have revealed that many routes are learned from older birds rather than being purely instinctive.

Tourism now accounts for roughly ten percent of global economic output and provides employment for hundreds of millions of people. While the industry brings income and investment to developing regions, it can also inflate local prices, damage fragile environments, and displace traditional communities. Sustainable tourism initiatives aim to balance these costs by directing visitor spending towards conservation and local businesses.

Artificial reefs, constructed from sunken ships, concrete blocks, and specially designed modules, provide hard surfaces where marine life can attach and flourish. Within a few years of deployment, these structures become colonised by corals, sponges, and fish, creating ecosystems that rival natural reefs in diversity. They also reduce fishing pressure on natural reefs by attracting divers and anglers elsewhere.

Nutrition science has moved far beyond simply counting calories. Researchers now study how the timing of meals, the diversity of gut bacteria, and the degree of food processing influence health outcomes. Highly processed foods, even when matched for calories with whole foods, appear to promote overeating, possibly because they are softer, quicker to consume, and engineered to be intensely flavourful.

retellLecture.title: How remote sensing monitors the planet
retellLecture.sample: The lecture explained how remote sensing satellites monitor the Earth. The speaker described how sensors measure reflected light and heat to detect deforestation, crop health, and urban growth. The technology has become cheaper and more detailed over time, and its images now support disaster response, such as mapping floods and wildfires within hours of an event.
retellLecture.text: Remote sensing means gathering information about the Earth from a distance, usually by satellites or aircraft. Modern satellites carry sensors that record not only visible light but also infrared and microwave radiation, allowing them to see through clouds and operate at night. By comparing images taken over time, scientists can detect deforestation in the tropics, measure how quickly glaciers are retreating, and estimate the health of crops across entire continents. The technology has improved dramatically: thirty years ago, each pixel in a satellite image covered an area the size of a football field, whereas today commercial satellites can distinguish objects smaller than a car. Remote sensing has also become essential in disaster response, helping emergency teams map floods, wildfires, and earthquake damage within hours, so that aid can be directed where it is needed most.

retellLecture.title: Why languages are disappearing
retellLecture.sample: The lecture discussed the rapid disappearance of languages worldwide. The speaker explained that one language dies out roughly every two weeks, usually when a small community shifts to a dominant language for economic reasons. The consequences include the loss of unique knowledge about plants and history. Finally, the speaker described revival efforts such as recording elders and teaching endangered languages in schools.
retellLecture.text: Of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken today, nearly half are considered endangered, and linguists estimate that one language falls silent every two weeks. Language loss usually happens gradually: younger generations switch to a dominant national language because it offers better education and employment, and within three generations the ancestral tongue may disappear entirely. The consequences go far beyond words. Every language encodes unique knowledge about local plants, weather patterns, and history, and this knowledge vanishes when the last speaker dies. Some communities, however, are fighting back. In New Zealand, Maori is now taught in immersion schools, and in Wales, government support has doubled the number of Welsh speakers under thirty. Technology helps too: linguists are recording the voices of elderly speakers and building digital archives before it is too late.

respondToSituation.prompt: You reserved a quiet study room in the library for a group project, but when you arrive, another group is sitting inside and refuses to leave. Your project meeting starts in five minutes. Speak to the other group. What would you say?
respondToSituation.audio: You reserved a quiet study room in the library for a group project, but when you arrive, another group is sitting inside and refuses to leave. Your project meeting starts in five minutes. Speak to the other group. What would you say?
respondToSituation.sample: Hi everyone, sorry to interrupt. I think there might be a mix-up — our group actually booked this room from three o'clock today. Here's the confirmation email on my phone with the room number and the time slot. Our project meeting starts in five minutes and we really need the space. If you don't have a booking, maybe I could help you find a free room — I think there are usually a couple available on the second floor, or you could ask at the front desk. I'd really appreciate it if you could pack up in the next couple of minutes so we can set up. Thanks a lot for understanding, and sorry for the hassle.

respondToSituation.sample: Hello Mr Davies, it's Maria from flat two. I'm calling about the rent increase notice I received yesterday. I've checked my contract, and it states that any increase requires at least two months' written notice, but this letter gives only two weeks, so I don't think it can legally take effect yet. Also, twenty percent is a very large jump — I'd struggle to afford that on my current budget. I'd like to suggest we meet and discuss a more gradual increase, perhaps spread over the next year. I've always paid on time and looked after the flat, so I hope we can reach an agreement that works for both of us. Could you call me back when you're free? Thank you.

summarizeGroupDiscussion.topic: Should public libraries lend tools and equipment, not just books?
summarizeGroupDiscussion.sample: The group discussed whether libraries should lend tools and equipment as well as books. Speaker A supported the idea, arguing that many people cannot afford items like drills or sewing machines and only need them occasionally. Speaker B raised concerns about insurance, safety, and maintenance costs, suggesting libraries partner with existing tool-sharing schemes instead. Speaker C proposed a compromise: starting with a small pilot collection of low-risk items such as board games and sewing kits. They agreed the concept had merit but required careful planning and funding.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: I think it's a brilliant idea. Most people use a power drill maybe twice a year, so why should every household buy one? Libraries already have the borrowing system in place — they'd just be extending it to objects people genuinely need.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: I love the principle, but the practical side worries me. Who's responsible if someone injures themselves with a library chainsaw? The insurance alone could be enormous, and tools need cleaning, sharpening, and repair. That's a whole new staff skillset.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Other cities manage it, though. There's a tool library in Toronto that's been running for years without major problems.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: Maybe we don't need to start with chainsaws. What if the library began with low-risk items — board games, sewing kits, telescopes, that kind of thing? A small pilot scheme would show whether people actually use it before we invest in expensive equipment.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: A pilot I could support. And perhaps we partner with the community centre rather than doing everything through the library itself — they already run repair workshops.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Partnering makes sense, as long as the items are free to borrow with a library card. The whole point is equal access.

summarizeGroupDiscussion.topic: The university wants to replace printed course readers with digital-only materials. Discuss.
summarizeGroupDiscussion.sample: The speakers debated replacing printed course readers with digital-only materials. Speaker A welcomed the change, citing lower costs, instant updates, and environmental benefits. Speaker B argued that many students concentrate better on paper and that screens cause eye strain during long reading sessions. Speaker C suggested a hybrid model where digital is the default but students can order printed copies at cost price. They concluded that a hybrid approach with an opt-out option would satisfy most students.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Honestly, this is long overdue. Digital readers cost a fraction of printed ones, lecturers can update them every semester instead of using outdated editions, and think of the paper we'd save. My printed reader last term cost forty pounds and I barely opened it.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: But that's exactly the problem — you barely opened it. Reading long texts on a screen is genuinely harder for a lot of people. I retain far more when I can physically highlight and flip pages. And after eight hours of lectures, the last thing my eyes need is more screen time.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: Both of you have a point. Why not make digital the default, which saves the university money, but let students order a printed copy at cost price if they prefer? The print shop on campus could handle orders in a day or two.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: I could live with that, provided the printed option isn't outrageously expensive and isn't quietly removed after a year.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Fine with me too, as long as nobody is forced to buy either version. Digital should be free, and print should be genuinely optional.

summarizeWrittenText.passage: Animal intelligence was once measured almost entirely by how closely a species' abilities resembled human skills, a bias that led scientists to underestimate many creatures. Recent research, however, has revealed sophisticated cognition in unexpected places. Octopuses, whose nervous systems evolved along an entirely different path from our own, can unscrew jars, navigate mazes, and recognise individual human faces. Crows manufacture hooked tools from twigs and plan for future needs, caching food according to what they expect to want the following morning. Even bees, with brains smaller than a pinhead, can learn the abstract concept of zero and count up to four. These findings have forced a fundamental rethink of what intelligence is. Rather than a single ladder with humans at the top, intelligence is increasingly viewed as a diverse set of solutions that evolution has produced in response to each species' particular ecological challenges, making cross-species comparison far more complex than previously assumed.
summarizeWrittenText.sample: Research revealing that octopuses, crows, and even bees possess sophisticated cognitive abilities has overturned the human-centred view of intelligence, which is now understood as a diverse collection of evolutionary solutions shaped by each species' specific ecological challenges rather than a single scale with humans at the top.

summarizeWrittenText.passage: Urban planning in the twentieth century was dominated by the principle of zoning, which separated residential, commercial, and industrial areas into distinct districts connected by roads. While this approach protected households from factory pollution, it produced sprawling cities in which daily life was impossible without a car. In recent decades, planners have increasingly embraced the concept of the fifteen-minute city, where homes, workplaces, shops, schools, and parks all lie within a short walk or bicycle ride. Advocates argue that such neighbourhoods reduce emissions, improve public health through daily physical activity, and strengthen local economies. Critics, however, warn that denser mixed-use districts can drive up property prices and displace lower-income residents unless affordable housing is protected. Several European cities are now testing the model by converting traffic lanes into cycling paths, creating pocket parks in former car parks, and permitting small shops to open within residential blocks.
summarizeWrittenText.sample: Although twentieth-century zoning created car-dependent sprawl, modern planners are adopting the fifteen-minute city concept, which promises lower emissions, better health, and stronger local economies by placing daily needs within walking distance, though critics caution that affordable housing must be protected to prevent the displacement of poorer residents.

summarizeSpokenText.title: What octopuses reveal about animal minds
summarizeSpokenText.sample: The lecture explored octopus intelligence. The speaker explained that octopuses evolved intelligence independently from vertebrates, with most of their neurons located in their arms rather than the brain. Experiments show they can solve puzzles, unscrew jars, and remember individual humans. The lecture concluded that studying octopuses helps scientists understand that intelligence can evolve along very different biological paths.
summarizeSpokenText.audio: The octopus offers a unique window into how intelligence can evolve. Our last common ancestor with the octopus was a simple worm-like creature that lived over five hundred million years ago, which means octopus intelligence developed entirely independently of our own. Most remarkably, two-thirds of an octopus's neurons are located not in its brain but in its arms, so each arm can process information and even make decisions on its own. In laboratory experiments, octopuses have learned to unscrew jars to reach food, navigate mazes from memory, and recognise individual human keepers, greeting familiar faces differently from strangers. In the wild, veined octopuses carry coconut shells around and assemble them into shelters, behaviour many scientists consider genuine tool use. Studying these animals matters because it shows intelligence is not a single human-style ability but a solution evolution can reach through completely different biological routes.

summarizeSpokenText.title: The economics of mass tourism
summarizeSpokenText.sample: The lecture examined the economic effects of mass tourism. The speaker explained that tourism creates jobs and foreign currency, but much of the profit leaks out to international hotel chains and cruise companies, with some destinations keeping only a small share of visitor spending. The lecture concluded that locally owned businesses and tourism taxes help destinations retain more of the money tourists bring.
summarizeSpokenText.audio: Tourism is frequently described as an economic miracle for developing countries, and it does bring clear benefits: it creates millions of jobs, earns foreign currency, and funds infrastructure such as airports and roads. However, economists have identified a serious problem known as leakage. In many popular destinations, the hotels belong to international chains, the tour operators are foreign-owned, and even the food served to tourists is imported. Studies of some Caribbean islands suggest that as much as eighty percent of tourist spending leaks straight back out of the local economy. Cruise ships present an extreme case: thousands of passengers spend a few hours ashore, buy little beyond a coffee and a souvenir, and then eat and sleep back on board. The lesson, economists argue, is not to reject tourism but to manage it, by supporting locally owned businesses, training local workers for skilled positions, and using tourist taxes to fund public services.
